title: Main Street Capital Access Act
official_title: To make improvements to the Federal banking laws, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: The sponsor is a Republican in the Republican-majority House, the bill carries 33 cosponsors, and it passed the House. The exemption of most sub-$10B bank mergers from antitrust review and the limits on guidance enforcement are likely to draw Democratic opposition in the Senate, where 60 votes would be required.
summary: This bill rewrites a broad range of federal banking laws to ease regulation of smaller banks, speed up new-bank formation, and limit how agencies use supervisory guidance. It raises several size thresholds, exempts most bank mergers under $10B from antitrust review, and orders studies of bank-fintech partnerships.
brief: Eases federal banking regulation for smaller institutions and exempts most bank mergers under $10B from antitrust review.

top_lines.headline: Community Bank Regulatory Relief
subs: Raises the Small Bank Holding Company threshold to $6B
Tailors capital and reporting rules for banks under $6B in assets

top_lines.headline: Bank Merger and Competition Changes
subs: Exempts most bank mergers under $10B from antitrust review
Adds merger-approval clarity and process reviews

top_lines.headline: Supervision and Guidance Limits
subs: Requires agencies to state their guidance is not legally binding
Shortens the regulatory-review cycle from 10 to 8 years
Cuts the new-bank de novo review period from 180 to 90 days

sections.label: Titles I-II - New Bank Formation and Regulatory Tailoring

items.main: Speeds new-bank formation and directs banking regulators to tailor rules to institutions' size and risk, raising the Small Bank Holding Company threshold to $6B.
items.detail: Cuts a new-bank de novo review period from 180 to 90 days and makes related pilot authorities permanent unless regulators find adverse safety effects in a 2031 review window. Regulators must publish annual charter-application data, and the Small Bank Holding Company Policy Statement asset threshold is raised to $6B. A new Section 177 of the Financial Stability Act indexes enhanced-regulation thresholds every 5 years.

items.main: Extends and adjusts the Community Development Financial Institutions bond-guarantee program.
items.detail: Sets the minimum guarantee at $25M with a $1B annual cap, changes the fee to between 10 and 15 basis points, and extends the program's authority to December 31, 2028. It also requires annual Treasury testimony on the Community Development Financial Institutions Fund.

sections.label: Titles III-IV - Bank Supervision and Guidance Accountability

items.main: Limits how financial agencies use supervisory guidance and adds supervision-process and accountability requirements.
items.detail: Requires nine financial agencies, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Department of Housing and Urban Development, to prominently state on any guidance that it does not have the force of law and does not bind regulated parties. It also adds fair-audit and appeals provisions for examinations and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation board accountability requirements, and shortens a regulatory review cycle from every 10 years to every 8 years.

sections.label: Titles V-VI - Local Bank Funding and Merger Clarity

items.main: Modernizes Federal Reserve discount-window access, promotes keeping deposits local, and eases bank merger review.
items.detail: For merger transactions resulting in an institution with less than $10B in assets that would not leave only one bank in a metropolitan area, the responsible agency may not consider whether the merger would create a monopoly or lessen competition. It also adds merger-approval timelines and a study of merger review procedures.

sections.label: Titles VII-VIII - Bank Resolution and Innovation

items.main: Changes bank-failure resolution rules and eases limits on merchant banking and bank-fintech partnerships.
items.detail: Sets the general holding period for merchant banking investments at no less than 15 years and orders studies of bank-fintech and credit-union-fintech partnerships. It also reduces the Federal Reserve's discretionary surplus fund by $425M effective September 1, 2036.

underreported.summary: Bars the responsible agency from considering monopoly or competition effects for bank and holding-company mergers resulting in institutions under $10B that would not leave only one bank in a metropolitan area.
underreported.why_unreported: The title is captioned as promoting competition and merger clarity, but this provision removes antitrust review for a class of mergers.

underreported.summary: Requires nine financial agencies to state on all guidance that it is not legally binding and that noncompliance does not establish a violation.
underreported.why_unreported: This reaches beyond banks to agencies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission and Housing and Urban Development, limiting how each enforces expectations set through guidance.

underreported.summary: Reduces the Federal Reserve's discretionary surplus fund amount by $425M, effective September 1, 2036.
underreported.why_unreported: This distant-dated reduction to the Federal Reserve surplus is a budget offset unrelated to the bill's stated banking-access purpose.

gaps: The bill aims to promote new bank formation but sets no target or deadline for reducing charter-application processing times, only requiring the agencies to report them.
The bill exempts most sub-$10B mergers from antitrust review but does not address the cumulative effect of successive exempt mergers on local competition.
The bill raises the Small Bank Holding Company threshold to $6B but, unlike the enhanced-regulation thresholds it indexes, does not index that threshold for future growth.
The bill orders studies of bank-fintech and credit-union-fintech partnerships but makes no change to the rules governing those partnerships.
The bill reduces the Federal Reserve discretionary surplus fund by $425M in 2036 but does not state how the resulting funds are used.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Loudermilk
featured_quotes.text: I obviously rise in support of H.R. 6955 not only because it is a good bill, but also because I recognize the need to rightsize Federal regulations and gain more transparency into the financial regulatory process. For too long, Federal financial regulators have taken this one-size- fits-all approach. If we applied that same status to ourselves, then let's just issue every Member of Congress one suit of clothes so that we all wear the same suit of clothes.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Velazquez
featured_quotes.text: Community banks and credit unions are the foundations of our financial system. As ranking member of the House Small Business Committee, I understand better than most the role they play in our communities, offering small business loans, farm loans, and mortgages. They are critical lifelines to our rural and underserved communities that have been left behind by our biggest banks.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Huizenga
featured_quotes.text: As a small business owner, I have seen it. I have lived it. When community banks disappear, families and small businesses lose the local lenders who know their communities and their customers best. Less competition means fewer financing options, higher borrowing costs, and less investment on Main Street, not Wall Street, as some of my colleagues are trying to assert. This bill lowers unnecessary regulatory costs for community and midsize banks, not those big business center banks on Wall Street and in New York and around the world.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Garcia
featured_quotes.text: I rise against H.R. 6955. Instead of the Main Street Act, this bill, Mr. Speaker, should be called the Wall Street wins Main Street loses act. It does not help end the affordability crisis, feed hardworking Americans, or keep a roof over their heads. Instead, this bill sneaks in deregulatory measures, further weakens the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and weakens community reinvestment and anti- discrimination safeguards. For this reason, at the appropriate time, I will offer a motion to recommit this bill back to committee.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Moylan
featured_quotes.text: When the people of Guam set out to enterprise new business ventures, we turn to our community banks to raise capital. However, much of America's financial system is not designed with small businesses in mind. While big banks have the resources to cut through red tape, small community ventures often struggle to comply with a regulatory regime that never had them in mind.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Knott
featured_quotes.text: For the vast majority of our Nation's history, community banks were the primary artery into progress for all Americans. That reality is being threatened today by sloppy and ineffective policies that originate right here in Washington, D.C. Whether it is the Dodd-Frank regulatory structure or the millions of rules and regulations that are in existence today, community banks have been choked out by these all-encompassing regulations. With administrative costs rising every year, local banks simply cannot afford to operate.

added: A requirement that nine financial agencies mark their guidance as non-binding (Section 402)
Annual charter- and deposit-insurance-application transparency reports by the banking regulators (Section 102)
Periodic indexing of enhanced-regulation thresholds (Section 177 of the Financial Stability Act)
A minimum 15-year merchant banking investment holding period and bank-fintech partnership studies (Sections 801-802)
modified: The Small Bank Holding Company Policy Statement asset threshold raised to $6B (Section 202)
The new-bank de novo review period cut from 180 days to 90 days (Section 101)
The Community Development Financial Institutions bond-guarantee minimum set at $25M with a $1B annual cap and authority extended to December 31, 2028 (Section 104)
The Federal Reserve discretionary surplus fund reduced by $425M effective September 1, 2036 (Section 803)
removed: Antitrust and competition review for bank and holding-company mergers resulting in institutions under $10B that would not leave only one bank in a metropolitan area (Section 601)
